blocks.text:
Design a news feed system, the system that shows each user a ranked stream of posts from the people and pages they follow, updated continuously as new posts arrive. The two problems that make this genuinely hard are not obviously related at first glance: how do you make reading a feed fast when a user might follow thousands of accounts, and how do you keep publishing a post fast when an account might have millions of followers, without either problem quietly making the other one worse.

The technique that resolves both problems at once is a hybrid fan-out strategy, pushing a post to followers immediately for ordinary accounts, but pulling a celebrity account's posts on demand instead, combined with a ranking score that blends recency, engagement, and personal affinity rather than showing posts in pure chronological order.

Design a news feed system, the system that shows each user a ranked stream of posts from the people and pages they follow, updated continuously as new posts arrive. The two problems that make this genuinely hard are not obviously related at first glance: how do you make reading a feed fast when a user might follow thousands of accounts, and how do you keep publishing a post fast when an account might have millions of followers, without either problem quietly making the other one worse.

The technique that resolves both problems at once is a hybrid fan-out strategy, pushing a post to followers immediately for ordinary accounts, but pulling a celebrity account's posts on demand instead, combined with a ranking score that blends recency, engagement, and personal affinity rather than showing posts in pure chronological order.

blocks.text: A user should be able to publish a post visible to their followers. A user should be able to view a ranked feed made up of posts from everyone they follow. New posts should appear in followers' feeds within a reasonably short time of being published. Feed ranking should take into account more than just recency, weighing engagement and the viewer's own history of interacting with a given author. A post from an account that has blocked or restricted a given viewer should never appear in that viewer's feed.

blocks.text: Five qualities matter here, and the first two are in direct tension with each other for exactly the accounts with the most followers.
blocks.content: Five qualities matter here, and the first two are in direct tension with each other for exactly the accounts with the most followers.

blocks.alt: Scalable fan-out, fast feed reads, relevance over pure chronology, reasonable freshness, and feed privacy

blocks.text: Scalable fan-out means publishing a single post can never mean writing to millions of follower feeds synchronously and instantly. Fast feed reads mean opening a feed cannot mean live-merging thousands of followed accounts' posts on every single request. Relevance over pure chronology means the single most recent post is not always the one most worth showing a viewer first. Reasonable freshness means a new post should reach followers' feeds within seconds, not requiring an exact, real-time guarantee. And feed privacy means a blocked or restricted relationship must be respected absolutely, a post must never leak into a feed it was never meant to reach, regardless of how well it would otherwise rank.

blocks.text: This design assumes a hybrid fan-out strategy is the right default, fan-out-on-write for accounts under a configured follower-count threshold, and fan-out-on-read for accounts above it, revisited as a trade-off in section 24. Feed ranking is assumed to blend recency, engagement, and a per-viewer affinity signal into a single score, rather than either pure chronological order or a black-box model. Blocking and content restrictions are assumed to be a hard filter applied before ranking, never something ranking itself can override.

blocks.text: A platform at real scale might have billions of users, the overwhelming majority of them with a modest follower count, alongside a comparatively tiny fraction of celebrity or page accounts with millions of followers each. Across the whole platform, hundreds of thousands of new posts might be published per second at peak, while feed reads happen far more often than posts are published, easily two orders of magnitude more frequently, which is exactly why fast reads matter as much as they do.

blocks.text: A new post goes to the post service, which checks the author's follower count against a celebrity threshold. Below it, fan-out workers push the post directly into every follower's own precomputed feed cache; above it, the post is simply stored, to be pulled directly at read time instead. When a viewer opens their feed, the feed read service combines their precomputed feed cache with posts pulled live from any celebrity accounts they follow, and a ranking service orders the combined result before it is returned.

blocks.alt: A post either fans out to every follower's precomputed feed cache, for an ordinary account, or is stored for later pull, for a celebrity account; a feed read merges both sources and ranks the result

blocks.text: For an ordinary account, a new post is pushed directly into every one of its followers' own precomputed feed caches the moment it is published, so that follower's future feed reads are simply fast cache reads, with no live computation needed at read time at all.

blocks.alt: An ordinary user's new post is pushed into every follower's own precomputed feed cache, making that follower's future feed reads simple, fast cache reads

blocks.text: For a celebrity account, pushing a new post to millions of followers' caches all at once would be prohibitively expensive. Instead, the post is simply stored once, and pulled directly by any follower who actually opens their feed, spreading the real cost across genuine reads rather than paying it all upfront on every single post.

blocks.alt: A celebrity account's post is never pushed to millions of follower caches; it is stored once and pulled directly by whichever followers actually open their feed

blocks.text: A candidate post's final ranking score blends how recently it was posted, how much engagement it has already received, and how often this specific viewer interacts with this specific author, so a slightly older but highly engaging or personally relevant post can reasonably outrank a very recent but otherwise unremarkable one.

blocks.text: The feed endpoint deliberately hides the underlying push-versus-pull split entirely, a client simply asks for a ranked feed and receives one, regardless of which fan-out strategy produced each individual post in it.

blocks.text: FeedCacheEntry's own rankScore column is deliberately stored rather than recomputed on every read, since a post's recency and engagement components change slowly enough that a periodically refreshed stored score is an acceptable, much cheaper approximation of a fully live recomputation.

blocks.text: The celebrity-threshold decision is evaluated once, at publish time, using the author's follower count at that exact moment, rather than being re-evaluated on every single fan-out or read, since a borderline account crossing the threshold mid-fan-out would otherwise create a genuinely ambiguous, half-pushed state. A user's affinity with a given author is maintained as its own lightweight, slowly-updated signal, rather than recomputed from raw interaction history on every single feed read.

blocks.alt: A new post is checked against the celebrity threshold, and, if below it, fanned out to every follower's own feed cache
A feed read combines already-pushed posts from the precomputed cache with posts pulled live from any followed celebrities, then ranks the combined result

blocks.text: The happy path for publishing is the publish flow above, an ordinary post fanned out cleanly to every follower's cache. The workflow worth walking through separately is a feed read for a user who follows both ordinary accounts and a celebrity, the feed read service does not treat these uniformly, it reads the precomputed cache for the ordinary side and separately, live, pulls from the celebrity's own post store, only merging and ranking the two result sets together at the very end, exactly the point where the hybrid strategy's two halves rejoin into one product experience.

blocks.alt: A returning user's already-ready precomputed feed cache is read directly and merged with any followed celebrities' posts; a brand-new user instead gets an initial feed built from scratch before ongoing maintenance begins

blocks.text: The precomputed feed cache is not a traditional cache invalidated on a TTL at all, it is a continuously-maintained materialized view, kept current by the fan-out workers themselves rather than expiring and being rebuilt from source on each read.
blocks.content: The precomputed feed cache is not a traditional cache invalidated on a TTL at all, it is a continuously-maintained materialized view, kept current by the fan-out workers themselves rather than expiring and being rebuilt from source on each read.

blocks.alt: A new ordinary post is placed on a fan-out queue, consumed by a worker pool that writes one entry per follower into their precomputed feed cache

blocks.text: Queuing fan-out work, rather than pushing to every follower synchronously within the publish request itself, is what keeps publishing fast regardless of how many followers an account happens to have, right up to the celebrity threshold.
blocks.content: Queuing fan-out work, rather than pushing to every follower synchronously within the publish request itself, is what keeps publishing fast regardless of how many followers an account happens to have, right up to the celebrity threshold.

blocks.alt: A feed read or fan-out write is routed to a feed-cache partition by hashing the affected user id, so every operation on one user's cache is always handled consistently

blocks.text: This keeps each user's own feed cache strictly local to one partition, letting fan-out writes and feed reads for that specific user proceed without needing any cross-partition coordination.
blocks.content: This keeps each user's own feed cache strictly local to one partition, letting fan-out writes and feed reads for that specific user proceed without needing any cross-partition coordination.

blocks.alt: A growing fan-out backlog or rising feed-read latency triggers adding more fan-out workers or feed-cache partitions

blocks.text: Because the celebrity threshold already caps how much fan-out work any single post can generate, scaling out fan-out workers and feed-cache partitions keeps pace with total platform growth without any single post ever becoming a uniquely enormous burst of work.
blocks.content: Because the celebrity threshold already caps how much fan-out work any single post can generate, scaling out fan-out workers and feed-cache partitions keeps pace with total platform growth without any single post ever becoming a uniquely enormous burst of work.

blocks.text: The precomputed feed cache is partitioned by user id and sized for the overwhelming majority of ordinary accounts' feeds. The post store, read directly for celebrity pull-based feeds, is partitioned by author id and replicated, since it directly serves live reads for exactly the accounts with the largest audiences.

The post store, read directly for celebrity pull-based feeds, is partitioned by author id and replicated, since it directly serves live reads for exactly the accounts with the largest audiences.

blocks.alt: How quickly a new post reaches a follower's feed is eventually consistent, a small, ordinary propagation delay; a post's exact ranking score is best-effort, a heuristic signal blend rather than a single provably correct value

blocks.text: Neither piece of state here demands strong, exact consistency, a feed that is a few seconds behind the very latest post, or a ranking that reasonable people could rank slightly differently, are both acceptable in a way that a genuinely lost post or a privacy leak never would be.

blocks.alt: A fan-out worker crashing partway through pushing one post to many followers safely resumes on the followers not yet reached, with a duplicate push to an already-reached follower being harmless rather than a real data-integrity problem

blocks.text: Making the fan-out write itself idempotent, pushing the same post twice to the same follower's cache has no different effect than pushing it once, is what turns a worker crash mid-fan-out into a routine, safely-retryable event rather than a risk of an inconsistent, partially-delivered post.

blocks.alt: A candidate post from an author who has blocked or restricted the viewer is excluded from that viewer's feed entirely, regardless of how well it would otherwise have ranked

blocks.text: Feed privacy is enforced as a hard filter applied before ranking ever runs, not as a low-scoring signal ranking could theoretically be overridden by, since a leaked post from a blocking relationship is a genuine trust and safety failure, not merely a relevance miss.

blocks.text: Fan-out queue depth and time-to-appear-in-feed are the clearest signals of whether ordinary post delivery is keeping pace with publishing volume. For celebrity accounts, feed-read latency specifically for viewers who follow one is worth its own dedicated monitoring, since that is exactly where the fan-out-on-read cost actually surfaces.

blocks.alt: A borderline account sitting right at the fan-out threshold, fan-out queue backlog during unusually high posting volume, and ranking computation cost growing with the number of candidate posts merged per feed read

blocks.text: The first of these is mitigated by choosing the celebrity threshold with real headroom, an account should not flip back and forth across the boundary from ordinary, everyday follower-count fluctuation, which would otherwise create a confusing, inconsistent fan-out history for that one account.

blocks.text: The hybrid approach is the right default because it refuses to let either extreme, an all-push or an all-pull design, take on a cost that scales with the platform's most extreme accounts, instead bounding each account's own worst case by which side of the threshold it falls on.
blocks.content: The hybrid approach is the right default because it refuses to let either extreme, an all-push or an all-pull design, take on a cost that scales with the platform's most extreme accounts, instead bounding each account's own worst case by which side of the threshold it falls on.

blocks.text: The celebrity threshold itself is the largest cost optimization in this design, converting what would otherwise be an unbounded, viral-post-driven fan-out cost into a bounded, predictable one. Storing a post's ranking score rather than recomputing it from scratch on every single feed read avoids repeating the same, slowly-changing computation far more often than its underlying signals actually change.

blocks.text: A change to the ranking formula's weighting needs careful, gradual rollout with real before-and-after engagement measurement, since a regression here is invisible to any simple health check yet directly affects what every single user sees on every visit. Adjusting the celebrity threshold itself needs particular care, since it can suddenly change the fan-out strategy for accounts sitting near the old boundary, and should be rolled out with monitoring for a fan-out cost spike.

blocks.text: A learned ranking model, trained on real engagement outcomes rather than a fixed, hand-tuned weighted formula, would likely improve relevance further than today's simpler blend. Real-time feed updates while a user is actively viewing their feed, rather than only on a fresh load, would make especially time-sensitive content, such as breaking news, feel more immediate.

items: Architecture: hybrid fan-out, push-on-write for ordinary accounts and pull-on-read for celebrity accounts, merged and ranked at feed-read time.
Capacity: billions of users with mostly modest follower counts, a tiny fraction of celebrity accounts, and feed reads outnumbering posts by roughly two orders of magnitude.

The core techniques: hybrid push/pull fan-out and a multi-signal ranking score blending recency, engagement, and affinity, both worked through with a real, verified implementation in Java, Python, and C++.
Database: a user-partitioned precomputed feed cache alongside an author-partitioned post store read directly for celebrity accounts.
End-to-end workflows: a normal publish-and-fan-out flow and a feed read merging both fan-out strategies, both traced as sequence diagrams.
Consistency: eventually consistent feed freshness paired with a best-effort, heuristic ranking score, with a hard, non-negotiable privacy filter applied before either.
Trade-offs: fan-out-on-write for everyone versus fan-out-on-read for everyone versus the hybrid approach, compared directly on publish cost and feed-read cost.
